name: Bole
confidence_why: Gimba's 2000 dissertation and 1998 thesis, the Gimba, Ali, Bah and Schuh 2009 dictionary and Schuh 2005 all describe Bole as a register tone language with two level tones and never mention stress, and Abraham's 1929 typescript, the only source that speaks of stress, defines stressed syllables simply as those carrying High tone, so the tonal reading rests on few but agreeing sources.

catalog_quote: 29. Bolenchi follows the same rules as Hausa for the inter-relation of tone and stress, i.e. stressed syllables have High Tone and unstressed syllables have Low Tone. They both employ three Falling Tones (I) High to Low. (2) Mid to below Low. (3) Low falling lower. ... Stress is marked after the syllable; the main stress is marked with " e.g. do"ki; secondary stress is marked witn ' e.g. tam"baya' (last syllable). Tones are marked below the syllable. There are three simple tones: High has no mark below the vowel, so all syllables having no mark below them are High Tone. Low Tone is indicated by a horizontal line below e.g. doki (High, Low). Mid Tone is marked by a small circle below e.g. kogi (Low, Mid).

new_statements.rule_in_words: In Abraham's 1929 (pre-phonemic, Hausa-modelled) analysis Bole has no stress independent of tone: a 'stressed' syllable is simply one bearing High tone and an 'unstressed' one bears Low tone, so 'stress' placement follows the lexical and grammatical tone melody of the word (e.g. Past-tense trisyllabic transitives High-Low-Mid vs intransitives Low-Mid-Low), not any positional rule. All modern descriptions (Gimba 1998, 2000; Gimba, Ali, Bah & Schuh 2009; Schuh's UCLA site) treat Bole as a two-tone (H/L) register language with downdrift, tone spreading and contrastive vowel length, and never mention stress at all.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Abraham marks a 'secondary stress' (') after the syllable, e.g. tam"baya' ('last syllable'), apparently corresponding to his Mid tone; no placement rule is given. Modern sources: none.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; Abraham lists tone-stress patterns by verb length and transitivity in the Past tense (disyllabic intransitives High-Low; trisyllabic transitives High-Low-Mid, intransitives mostly Low-Mid-Low with a few High-High-Low; quadrisyllabic transitives usually Low-Mid-Low-Mid). Modern work (Gimba 1998, 2000; dictionary 2009) describes Low Tone Raising and 'variable tone' words (phrase-final H-L becoming H-H medially).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (verb forms and nouns in isolation), Fika variety; Abraham's 'stress' is a tone correlate, not a separately measured prominence. The authoritative modern primary description (Gimba 2000, p. 8: 'Bole is a register tone language.. two level tones, high (H) and low (L)', file) is silent on stress; an instrumental study of Bole intonation (Schuh, Gimba & Ritchart 2010) exists but could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Fika (Fikka) variety of Bole (Abraham 1929: 'the language.. spoken at Fikka'; 2009 dictionary: 'based on the variety of Bole spoken in Fika'); Schuh 1983 (not opened) describes the Gadaka dialect. Glottolog nucl1695 has no separate dialect glottocodes for Fika/Bara. Abraham's 'Bolenchi/Bolanci' = Bole.

new_statements.quote: [p. 226, Abstract] The Bole tone system has two contrasting level tones, high (H) and low (L), which may be combined on heavy syllables to produce phonetic rising and falling tones. The prosody of intonation refers to lexical tones and the overall function of the utterance. Bole does not have lexical or phrasal stress, and intonation does not play a pragmatic role typical of stress languages, such as pitch raising to signal focus. [p. 235, sec. 1.4] Bole prosodic phenomena, in general, refer only to tone and intonation. The intonational patterns discussed in §§1.1-3 make no reference to syntax, and stress is not an independent prosodic feature of Bole. Even in the initial syllable sequences mu goj- … and shi ko-… in Figures 26 and 28, one does not hear the cues of stress-based iambs that one would hear, for example, in English.

This is a different prosodic type from Abraham's tone-equals-stress account (which reflects the 1920…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bole is a two-tone (H/L) register tone language with contour tones only on heavy syllables; the authors state outright that Bole has no lexical or phrasal stress and that stress is not an independent prosodic feature; all prosody is tone plus phrase-level intonation (downdrift, final lowering, initial H raising, appended XH/HL boundary tones), and focus is never marked prosodically.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; the work denies stress at any level. The only prominence-like remark is that phrase-initial clitics (mu 'we', shi 'you fs') start at slightly lower pitch and amplitude than their host, which the authors tentatively call 'reduction in prominence' of clitics, explicitly not a stress-based iambic effect, and flag as based on little, uncontrolled data (p. 235-236).
new_statements.exceptions: No stress exceptions. Tonal/intonational specifics: contour (falling H+L, rising L+H) tones restricted to heavy syllables; ideophones and ideophonic adjectives surface with extra-high tone phrase-finally, analysed as intonational rather than lexical (sec. 7); yes/no questions suspend downdrift and append XH; pleas append H+L.
new_statements.identity_note: Schuh, Gimba & Ritchart 2010 describe Bole as spoken in Yobe and Gombe States; the Yobe Languages Research Project materials (and co-author Gimba) are based on the Fika (Pikka) variety of Bole, the standard/orthographic variety. Abraham 1929 'Bolenchi' is the same language (Bolanci), Fika emirate.

tone_statements.quote: This paper presents the results of laboratory experiment on downdrift in Bole. Bole is a Chadic language of the West-A Branch (Newman 1977). It is spoken in Gombe and Yobe States of Nigeria. Bole has two lexical tones: high (H) and low (L). Like many Chadic languages, Bole has a downdrift phenomenon where the actual pitches of words descend such that a high following a low is lower than the preceding high (Silverstein 1976, Pierrehumbert and Beckman 1988, Leben 1989).
tone_statements.summary: Two level lexical tones, H and L; pitch-track study (51 tokens) of the domain of automatic downdrift (H after L lower than the preceding H), argued to be the Intermediate Phrase; Low Tone Raising (L syllable raised after H) cited from Gimba 1998. No phonemic downstep claimed; nothing on stress.

readall_conflicts: No new source contradicts anything. The only work actually read (Gimba 2000/2002 dissertation) describes Bole as a register tone language with two level tones and never mentions stress, which is compatible with the tone half of the only existing stress statement (Abraham 1929: stressed syllables carry High tone, unstressed Low tone) but gives no support for treating Bole as having word stress at all. The tension is one of description rather than data: Abraham's 1929 typescript equates 'stress' with high tone, while every modern Yobe-project description held by the project (Gimba 1998, 2000; Gimba & Schuh 2009; Schuh 2005 BLS) speaks only of tone. The three works that could settle it (Schuh, Gimba & Ritchart 2010 on intonation; Schuh's 2005 draft reference grammar; Frajzyngier 1987) could not be opened here. No new source was opened, so no new conflict arises. The standing disagreement held by the project remains: the catalog codes Bole 'tonal' from Abraham 1929 (stress correlated with High tone, Hausa-style, with main and secondary stress marks), while Schuh, Gimba & Ritchart 2010 (read earlier) state that Bole has no lexical or phrasal stress; Schuh's 2005 draft grammar, which would likely settle the modern analysis, could not be obtained. One disagreement: Abraham 1929 (typescript, §29 and 'Method of Transcription') describes Bolanci as having stress correlated with tone in the Hausa manner (stressed syllables High, unstressed Low) and marks main and secondary stress in hi…

sources.note: Earliest tonological paper on Bole: classifies consonants as 'tone-permeable' vs 'tone-impermeable', i.e. (per Gimba 2000: 'Lukas (1969) was the first to document a process in Bole by which a low tone becomes high when preceded by high') H spreads across a word boundary onto a following L unless the L syllable begins with a blocking (voiced obstruent, depressor-type) consonant; presupposes the two-tone H/L system. German, 6 pp.
